papers.title: rhythmCI: an R package for rhythm detection using harmonic regression amplitude confidence intervals
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are evolutionarily conserved systems that orchestrate daily rhythms in human physiology, tissue behavior, and cellular function. In circadian research, the NanoString nCounter platform has emerged as a robust alternative to microarray and RNA sequencing. However, raw instrument output requires specialized preprocessing to handle technical noise. Furthermore, while harmonic regression is widely used to detect periodic signals in biological time-series data, evaluating rhythmicity remains highly challenging in clinical studies characterized by sparse sampling and small sample sizes. To address these limitations, we developed rhythmCI, an easy-to-use R package that integrates established normalization methods with a complete workflow for circadian data analysis. The package incorporates a bootstrapping procedure to estimate confidence intervals for harmonic regression amplitudes, offering a statistically transparent way to quantify rhythmicity in small-cohort studies. rhythmCI provides an end-to-end workflow for NanoString nCounter data, including automated preprocessing, normalization, and visualization. We evaluated the utility and accuracy of the package using synthetic time-series data generated with the Simphony framework, demonstrating that rhythmCI produces interpretable and reliable rhythmicity classifications under controlled simulation conditions. rhythmCI bridges a critical gap in circadian bioinformatics by offering a reliable method to characterize periodicity under challenging experimental designs typical of clinical research. By streamlining NanoString workflows and improving the statistical rigor of rhythm detection in small datasets, rhythmCI enhances the accessibility and reliability of circadian biology analysis.

papers.title: Motor effort biases perceptual decisions through later-stage evidence accumulation rather than early sensory-attentional processing
papers.abstract: Motor effort has been shown to bias perceptual decisions toward less effortful choices, but it remains unknown whether this bias already takes effect during the early stages of decision formation through preparatory attentional allocation or sensory processing, or during later-stage evidence accumulation preceding response execution. This study investigated when motor effort becomes integrated into decision formation by focusing on the temporal evolution of neural processing during perceptual decision-making. While 64-channel EEG was recorded, twenty-four healthy adults performed an orientation discrimination task in which two Gabor patches appeared simultaneously in the left and right visual hemifield and decisions were reported using two pressure-sensitive response buttons requiring different levels of force. We found that motor effort modulated EEG activity at both the preparatory and later decision stages: pre-stimulus alpha power was reduced over the occipito-parietal cortex contralateral to the low-effort option, and mean centro-parietal positivity (CPP) amplitude preceding response execution was greater over centro-parietal cortex for low-effort choices, while leaving early sensory representations intact as indicated by no differences in P1 or N1 amplitude following stimulus onset. Trial-by-trial CPP amplitude preceding response execution increased with the likelihood of selecting the low-effort option, whereas the pre-stimulus alpha modulation was not associated with behavioral decision bias. These findings suggest that motor effort biases perceptual decisions primarily during later-stage evidence accumulation, thereby providing insight into the neural basis of embodied perceptual decision making.

papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo
papers.abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo. Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo.

papers.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response
papers.abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

papers.title: Acoustic Context Shapes Cortical Encoding of Spectral Discrimination in Normal and Impaired Hearing
papers.abstract: The auditory change complex (ACC) provides a cortical measure of acoustic discrimination, yet the mechanisms shaping responses to spectrotemporally complex sounds remain poorly understood. We investigated how acoustic context and temporal-envelope variability influence cortical encoding of spectral contrast in normal-hearing (NH) and hearing-impaired (HI) listeners. Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to record ACCs and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) evoked by spectrotemporally modulated stimuli. We compared conventional spectro-temporal modulations (STMs) with a novel discrete spectro-temporal modulation (DSTM) paradigm, examined temporal roving, and evaluated cortical responses to spectral contrast in NH and HI listeners. ACCs elicited by DSTM stimuli were larger and more symmetrical across transition directions than those elicited by conventional STMs. Temporal roving markedly reduced responses to intensity changes while largely preserving responses to spectral changes, indicating a partial dissociation between intensity-driven and spectrally driven cortical discrimination. ACC responses decreased systematically with spectral contrast and were weaker and delayed in HI listeners. By contrast, ASSRs remained highly detectable and showed no systematic dependence on spectral contrast, supporting a distinction between contrast-sensitive cortical discrimination and ongoing envelope encoding. Temporal roving further enhanced separation between NH and HI listeners. ACC response strength was significantly associated with behavioural STM discrimination thresholds and explained variance beyond age and audiometric thresholds. These findings demonstrate that cortical representations of spectral discrimination are shaped by acoustic context and temporal-envelope statistics. Temporal roving attenuates intensity-driven responses while preserving spectrally driven discrimination, providing insight into cortical encoding of spectrotemporal contrast and its relationship to perceptual performance.

papers.title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.

papers.title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm.
papers.abstract: Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.

papers.title: Neprilysin 1 in the Mushroom Body controls Feeding behavior by regulating SIFamide levels in Drosophila melanogaster
papers.abstract: Feeding-related behavior in Drosophila melanogaster encompasses olfactory and gustatory detection of odors, foraging, and food intake. In Drosophila melanogaster, the neuropeptide SIFamide (SIFa), has been shown to integrate hunger signals to promote feeding in Drosophila and is considered a central regulator of mutually exclusive behavioral states. Here, we identify the mushroom bodies as a key downstream circuit of SIFamidergic neurons for regulation of food-seeking and feeding. Furthermore, we show that mushroom bodies are not merely downstream effectors but actively shape SIFamidergic signaling through the peptidase Neprilysin 1 for which SIFamide is a substrate. Thus, SIFa signaling is embedded within a feedforward-feedback circuit that couples internal state to the selection and execution of feeding behavior. We propose that the distinct neuronal subtypes postsynaptic to the elaborately arborized SIFamidergic neurons define discrete neuronal subroutines that differentially control the mutually exclusive behaviors related to sexual reproduction, sleep and feeding. Our findings reveal an evolutionary ancient peptidergic system that is modified by recruitment of novel genes for the flexible control of distinct behavioral programs and feeding strategies.

papers.title: What EEG doesn't see: a whole-brain MEG map of sleep spindles and slow oscillations
papers.abstract: Sleep spindles and slow oscillations (SOs) are hallmarks of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, linked to memory consolidation and restorative functions. They are usually detected in one or a few scalp electroencephalography (EEG) channels with parameters that vary across studies, and serve as the reference even in magnetoencephalography (MEG), fMRI and intracranial studies. We argue that these choices filter which neural activity is captured. Nineteen young adults took a daytime nap during simultaneous MEG and EEG. Using MEG source imaging across 416 cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions, we mapped the amplitude and density of SOs (0.5-4 Hz, and 0.5-2 and 2-4 Hz separately) and of spindles (9-18 Hz, and slow, 9-12.9 Hz, and fast, 13-18 Hz, separately), and related each region's activity to a single scalp derivation (Cz-M1). Both rhythms were detected throughout the brain, including the thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia and cerebellum. The balance between bands varied across regions: fast spindles predominated over slow spindles along the dorsal midline, around the central sulcus and in the thalamus, slow spindles predominated in occipital cortex and the cerebellar hemispheres, and 2-4 Hz SOs were relatively most prominent in occipital cortex. Amplitude and density formed reliable but distinct maps: regions with larger fast spindles also had more of them, whereas SOs, and slow spindles once source depth was controlled, were larger where they were less frequent. More SOs were detected in every region than at Cz-M1, whereas more fast spindles were detected at Cz-M1 than in any single region. Around the SO, slow-spindle activity had the same timing at the scalp and in the sources, but the up-state increase in fast-spindle activity seen at the scalp was absent from local sources. Slow spindles were the most strongly shared events, and sensorimotor sources the most scalp-like. Thus, a single scalp derivation offers a selective and partly composite view of sleep oscillations, with implications for interpreting their functional roles and for targeting them with closed-loop auditory stimulation

papers.title: Intersectional genetic targeting of molecularly distinct melanin-concentrating hormone neuron subpopulations reveals distinct and overlapping subcircuit architecture
papers.abstract: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) coordinates crucial and innate behaviors through heterogeneous yet poorly understood neuronal populations and circuits. Neurons that produce melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH; encoded by the Pmch gene) are primarily localized in the LHA and contribute to feeding, sleep-wake regulation, memory, and reward-associated behaviors. Building on foundational anatomical studies, our single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the LHA identified markers distinguishing at least two transcriptionally distinct MCH subpopulations. These subpopulations are distinguished by the selective enrichment of the Tacr3 and Cartpt transcripts, with each comprising approximately half of the total MCH population. However, these subpopulations remain poorly understood owing to limited genetic targeting tools. We hypothesized that MCH neurons operate through functionally distinct, parallel subcircuits that exhibit unique neuroanatomical projections. In this study, we leveraged Pmch and Tacr3 expression to intersectionally dissociate these neurons into Type I MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3+) and Type II MCH (Pmch+/Tacr3-) subpopulations. We first validated a Tacr3-Flpo mouse line for the genetic targeting of the Type I MCH subpopulation. We then generated an intersectional Type I MCH neuron reporter line to visualize Type I axonal projections. In parallel, we injected a dual recombinase mouse line with the intersectional genetic targeting viruses, Conditional Viral Expression by Ribozyme Guided Degradation (ConVERGD), and identified overlapping and distinct projections by Type I and Type II MCH neurons using fluorescence microscopy, super-resolution imaging, and high-spatial resolution fiber mapping. Overall, these data establish the first subpopulation-resolved anatomical framework for molecularly distinct Type I and Type II MCH subcircuits, thus establishing a foundation for future circuit-level functional studies.

papers.title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
papers.abstract: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle's responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila, pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that dFic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation.

papers.title: Neurite Complexity and Plasticity Markers Track Synaptic Vesicle Density in the Living Human Brain: A Multimodal PET-MRI-EEG Study
papers.abstract: Neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise its structure and function, is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases and a putative mechanism of action for pharmacological interventions. [11C]-UCBJ positron emission tomography (PET), which quantifies synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) density, offers the most direct in vivo measure of human synaptic density, but its relationship to complementary, more scalable neuroimaging measures of structural and functional plasticity remains uncharacterised. We combined [11C]-UCBJ PET, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI/NODDI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG)-based sensory tasks (roving mismatch negativity, MMN; visual long-term potentiation, vLTP) in 18 healthy volunteers to test the relationship between synaptic terminal SV2A density and complementary structural and functional neuroplasticity measures, and whether these relationships were reproducible following pharmacological challenge with ketamine (n = 11) or N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT; n = 7). There were no statistically significant differences in PET-derived SV2A binding potential (BPND), DWI-derived neurite orientation dispersion (ODI) and structural weighted degree (SWD), EEG-derived MMN repetition suppression, and late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation, 1 to 8 days following DMT and ketamine exposure compared to baseline. BPND was coupled with ODI across cortical regions before and after pharmacological challenge, and this relationship was tighter within visual, attentional, and frontoparietal control brain networks. SWD showed a weaker, more spatially restricted association with BPND, primarily in regions belonging to the limbic and visual brain networks, but was not replicated post-drug. No consistent association was found between BPND and functional weighted degree (FWD), derived from rs-fMRI, at baseline or after pharmacological challenge. Frontotemporal BPND was positively associated with MMN repetition suppression (r = 0.61), and occipital BPND with late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation (r = 0.54), with the MMN-BPND association replicating after pharmacological challenge (r = 0.49). These findings link synaptic terminal SV2A density in the living human brain to neurite architecture and the capacity for short-term and Hebbian-like long-term synaptic plasticity, while dissociating these relationships from generic functional connectivity and magnitude of sensory-evoked responses. These data provide cross-modal validation for DWI- and EEG-derived measures as biological indices and surrogate measures of human synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: A hippocampal digital Twin reveals latent structure in freely flying bats
papers.abstract: Concurrent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale neuronal recording, and behavioral tracking have enabled increasingly powerful predictive models of brain-behavior relationships. Yet predictive accuracy does not automatically yield interpretable principles of neural organization, particularly during natural behavior, where the relevant variables computed are often unknown in advance. Here, we developed a functional digital twin of the hippocampus, trained jointly on large-scale neural activity and self-directed three-dimensional flight in freely flying bats. A multimodal, multitask transformer accurately predicted both neural activity and behavior, outperformed standard approaches, and generalized across recording sessions. Interrogating the model's representations suggested a form of hippocampal generalization across self-selected trajectories that was not apparent in physical coordinates, but was plainly visible in the model's low-dimensional latent space. We confirmed this organization directly in the recorded neural activity: neurons fired at corresponding stages of spatially distinct paths connecting the same origin and destination, preserving their relative firing order even as their firing fields shifted with the path. Analysis of neuron-specific readouts further identified functional relationships among neurons that generalized from flight to waking rest and sleep, brain states never used for training, and differed systematically between the hippocampal subregions CA1 and CA3. Together, these results show how AI-based functional digital twins can complement conventional analysis by generating testable hypotheses about neural organization during natural behavior.

papers.title: Chronic Electrophysiology Captures Progressive Variability in DNA-Damaged Cardiac Networks
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological recordings provide a key functional readout of cardiac health. Most in vitro studies rely on acute measurements rather than recording evolving functional changes. Here, we implement a microelectrode array (MEA) based system for chronic electrophysiological monitoring of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (iPSC-CM) monolayers. Electrophysiology recordings were maintained for up to 40 days, enabling longitudinal assessment of field potential amplitude, field potential duration, beat frequency, conduction velocity, and waveform morphology. Untreated iPSC-CM monolayers exhibited stable electrophysiological behavior throughout chronic culture. Following exposure to the cardiotoxic chemotherapeutic doxorubicin, chronic recordings captured progressive deterioration in electrical activity, including reduced field potential amplitude, altered repolarization dynamics, increased beat-to-beat variability, and reduced conduction that persisted after drug removal. Electrode-resolved analyses further revealed pronounced progressive spatial variability, highlighting localized responses that would be obscured by population-averaged measurements. Endpoint assays indicated reduced calcium transient amplitude and altered calcium reuptake, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, and loss of connexin 43, findings consistent with the impaired electrical activity observed in chronic recordings. Together, these results establish chronic electrophysiological monitoring as a powerful approach for resolving the spatiotemporal progression of cardiotoxicity and other dynamic cardiac processes in vitro.

papers.title: Selective Auditory Attention Decoding with a Two-Node Wireless EEG Sensor Network
papers.abstract: Objective. Selective auditory attention decoding (sAAD) enables neuro-steered hearing devices by identifying the attended speaker in a multi-speaker environment from neural activity recorded with electroencephalography (EEG). Despite algorithmic progress, practical deployment remains constrained by a lack of wearable, unobtrusive, and fully wireless EEG acquisition solutions. We therefore evaluate whether reliable sAAD can be achieved under the realistic hardware constraints of a wireless EEG sensor network (WESN) of miniaturized, galvanically isolated EEG sensor nodes. Approach. We use a WESN of two synchronized, compact around-ear EEG sensor nodes worn bilaterally. Each node provides four local EEG channels derived from five pre-gelled electrodes, including a local reference. Sample-wise wireless synchronization of data from both nodes enables joint processing as an eight-channel EEG. On a newly recorded dataset, we apply correlation-based stimulus decoding, followed by hidden Markov model (HMM)-based post-processing. Main results. Stimulus decoding achieves an average sAAD accuracy of 69.24% on 60s decision windows, comparable to previously reported wired around-ear EEG systems that measure long-distance scalp potentials. HMM-based post-processing further improves this to a steady-state accuracy of 77.17% with an average simulated attention switch detection time of 32.79s. Combining sensor nodes at both ears outperforms single-ear configurations, primarily through redundancy rather than complementary spatial information. Finally, a fixed bipolar configuration using four electrodes per ear, yielding three channels, suffices to maintain performance. Significance. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of sAAD using a fully wireless, galvanically isolated around-ear WESN and establish a realistic performance benchmark under practical hardware constraints.

papers.title: Hypoxia Disrupts Multiple Processes Supporting Spatial Navigation
papers.abstract: Hypoxia impairs cognitive function, yet its effects on navigation and intrinsic brain activity remain poorly understood. This study investigated whether a continuous exposure to hypoxia (CH) or an intermittent exposure to hypoxia (IH) differentially influence navigation performance and resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) in healthy young adults. Seventy-two participants completed sham (FiO2 = .209) and hypoxia (FiO2 = .13) sessions during either a one hour of CH or IH intervention. Navigation was assessed using the Spatial Performance Assessment for Cognitive Evaluation (SPACE), while resting-state EEG was recorded before and after the intervention in a subset of participants (n = 40). EEG spectra were parameterised into periodic (alpha and beta power and central frequency) and aperiodic (exponent and offset) components. Aligned rank transform (ART) analyses of variance examined effects of hypoxia and intervention group, while linear regression determined whether reductions in peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) predicted changes in navigation or EEG. Hypoxia impaired multiple components of navigation, increasing path integration distance error and egocentric pointing angle error irrespective of intervention group, while mapping accuracy was preferentially impaired following IH and perspective taking performance following CH. Hypoxia also reduced alpha and beta power, beta central frequency, and aperiodic exponent, while aperiodic offset and alpha central frequency remained stable. The reduction in aperiodic exponent was primarily evident following IH, suggesting that the temporal pattern of oxygen delivery may influence specific neurophysiological responses. Contrary to our hypothesis, SpO2 reduction did not predict individual differences in navigation performance or EEG activity. These findings demonstrate that brief, moderate hypoxic exposure can disrupt allocentric and egocentric components of spatial navigation while selectively altering periodic and aperiodic features of intrinsic brain activity.

papers.title: Dizocilpine-derived K2060 exhibits enhanced blockage at NMDA receptors with impaired Mg2+ block and provides strong protection against audiogenic seizures
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose: Voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is a defining feature of the GluN1/GluN2 subtype of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs). We tested how impaired Mg2+ block at GluN1/GluN2A receptors mutated at the GluN2A-N615 position modifies inhibition by dizocilpine-derived K2060 compared with clinically used memantine and ketamine. Experimental Approach: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on recombinant wild-type (WT) and mutated GluN1/GluN2A receptors expressed in HEK293T cells. Acute hippocampal slice electrophysiology and behavioural studies were conducted in WT and knock-in GluN2A-N615S mice. In vivo tolerability and efficacy were evaluated using open field testing, prepulse inhibition (PPI), and protection against audiogenic seizures (AGS). Key Results: Mg2+ reduced the apparent potency of all three blockers and slowed onset at the GluN1/GluN2A-WT receptor. These Mg2+-dependent effects were absent or markedly reduced at the GluN1/GluN2A-N615S and GluN1/GluN2A-N615K receptors. In addition, K2060 showed slower unbinding and greater trapping than memantine. In hippocampal slices from GluN2A-N615S mice, K2060 exhibited enhanced but slower onset inhibition than memantine and ketamine. In vivo, K2060 caused no overt behavioural disruption at 5 mg/kg (i.p.) and did not further disrupt PPI. All three blockers protected GluN2A-N615S mice against AGS at 5 mg/kg (i.p.); only K2060 remained protective at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). Conclusions and Implications: Impaired Mg2+; block removes a physiological constraint on the action of NMDAR blockers. K2060 exhibited the most favourable pharmacological profile, supporting its further evaluation for studies with NMDAR hyperfunction models. Additional pharmacokinetic, safety, and disease-model studies are warranted.

papers.title: Hyperglycaemia reversibly disrupts circadian behaviour in mice
papers.abstract: Disrupted sleep and circadian rhythms are among the most common features of diabetes, and are known to raise the risk of developing the disease. Whether the relationship also runs the other way, with diabetes itself disrupting the clock, has remained unresolved. Using an inducible mouse model of diabetes, in which hyperglycaemia can be induced and then reversed within the same animal, we show that elevated blood glucose is a reversible cause of circadian disruption. Raising blood glucose reduced the amplitude of circadian rest-activity rhythms by 50%, in proportion to the degree of hyperglycaemia, and shortened the free-running period of the clock. Restoring normoglycaemia reversed both effects. Diabetic animals had a delayed phase of activity onset, i.e. later chronotype, and re-entrained more slowly after a simulated jet lag. However, phase shifting to nocturnal light pulses was intact, suggesting normal photic responses. Brain glucose and O-GlcNAcylation, a nutrient-sensitive protein modification, were both elevated in diabetic animals, showing that peripheral hyperglycaemia reaches the brain and alters its metabolic state, and providing a molecular readout of that exposure. Together, these findings establish that a peripheral metabolic state is a reversible determinant of circadian rest-activity behaviour, completing a bidirectional link between blood glucose and the clock and arguing that the two must be treated together rather than in isolation.

papers.title: Sleep-dependent modulation of thalamic brain temperature estimates in humans
papers.abstract: Mammalian thermal physiology is geared towards dissipating heat during sleep. Brain temperature typically decreases during non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep in all mammalian species measured to date, yet non-invasive confirmation in healthy humans is lacking: the only available human study used invasive recordings in epileptic patients without a wake control condition. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables brain temperature mapping non-invasively, using the temperature-sensitive chemical shift of water relative to N-Acetyl-Aspartate as an internal reference. First, we validated that with metabolite cycling (MC), a MRS approach that enables the simultaneous acquisition of metabolite and water information without conventional water suppression, can be used to determine estimates of brain temperature in an ex vivo sheep head. Next, we determined that by using a temporal resolution of ~4 minutes, we obtained high-quality spectra without losing excessive temporal resolution. We then re-analyzed an existing set of MRS data (acquired with the MC sequence) of the thalamus in young adults (n=9) who slept in the evening for up to 2 hours in the scanner, to assess sleep-evoked changes in estimates of brain temperature. Of the nine participants, five participants took part in the subsequent wake-only experiment, allowing to control for the potential impact of circadian time and body posture on estimates of brain temperature. Sleep-wake states were quantified with standard polysomnography, confirming that the participants managed to sleep in the scanner. On average, they spent 39.4+/-15.7 min in N2 sleep, 24.8+/-18.1 min in N3 sleep, 10.0+/-4.9 min in N1 sleep, and 37.0+/-19.6 min awake. Estimates of brain temperature were correlated across the sleep and wake-only experiment within the same participant (R^2=0.29, P<0.0001). When participants entered NREM sleep, estimates of brain temperature decreased by 0.2 degrees Celcius. Moreover, the deeper NREM sleep, the more pronounced the decrease in estimates of brain temperature (P=0.014). These data suggest that an evening nap consisting of NREM sleep decreases thalamic temperature. Considering the profound impact temperature can have on brain functioning, these brain temperature changes could be a pathway through which sleep impacts the brain.

papers.title: ScreenDMT reveals metabolites replicably associated with sleep disorders across three human cohorts
papers.abstract: The robust replication of scientific findings across independent studies is essential, yet it remains challenging in high-dimensional biological datasets. A critical aspect of true replication requires detecting not only the repeated presence but also the consistent direction of an effect. Traditional methods for evaluating replication often ignore effect directionality or lack adequate statistical power when adjusting for multiple comparisons. To address this, we extend the directional MaxP test (DMT) and our screening-integrated procedure, ScreenDMT, to evaluate directional replication across an arbitrary number of independent studies. We mathematically prove ScreenDMT's validity for an arbitrary number of studies when the studies' sample sizes grow unbounded. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate that ScreenDMT effectively controls error rates, such as the false discovery rate (FDR), in finite sample sizes and yields higher statistical power than competing methods especially for three studies. We applied the extended ScreenDMT to untargeted blood metabolomics profiles across three diverse human cohorts - ARIC (N=1,337), MESA (N=1,874), and HCHS/SOL (N=6,180) - to discover replicable biomarkers for dichotomous insomnia, long sleep, short sleep, and excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). We found low levels of cortisol to be replicably associated with EDS, and high levels of n-formylmethionine to be associated with long sleep. Furthermore, directional pathway analysis revealed that low levels of xanthine metabolites are replicably associated with insomnia. These convergent findings validate ScreenDMT as a powerful methodology for simultaneous multi-cohort replication and offer robust insights into the metabolic signatures underlying sleep disorders across diverse populations.
